Gastroenterology · published research

Anal fistula

A mixed postoperative study reported greater wound-width reduction with near-infrared treatment, but fistula-specific closure was not established and length results varied. In rats, PBM reduced tract area and inflammatory findings without closing the fistula.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A mixed postoperative study reported greater wound-width reduction with near-infrared treatment, but fistula-specific closure was not established and length results varied. In rats, PBM reduced tract area and inflammatory findings without closing the fistula.

Summary of the Evidence

Two relevant publications are identified: one nonrandomized human study of postoperative perianal wounds that included fistula cases alongside abscess and hemorrhoid surgery, and one rat fistula-in-ano experiment. The human report is a narrow related-category mapping, not a fistula-only trial; its fistula subgroup denominator and diagnosis-specific closure outcome are not clearly established. The two papers are separate human and animal experiments.

Human and clinical evidence

The human study compared near-infrared PBM plus routine care with a control approach across mixed anorectal wounds. In the combined sample, wound width decreased by 46% in the PBM group and 26% in controls, while wound length decreased by 35% and 30%, respectively. The paper’s fistula-specific description reports a greater reduction in width with PBM but a greater length reduction in controls. Because wound types were mixed, follow-up was only five days, and fistula-specific closure and recurrence were not measured, these dimensional changes do not establish fistula healing (Nurfitri et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

In a rat fistula model, daily red-light laser treatment for 30 days reduced remaining tract area, inflammatory-cell infiltration, and vascular congestion compared with untreated animals. No tract closed completely. The results therefore show reduced tract size and local inflammation in this model, not full fistula resolution (Dos Santos et al. 2021).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No exact-category cell-culture or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human wound study used 808-nm near-infrared light at 100 mW/cm² for 15 minutes on days 0, 1, 2, 3, and 5. It did not report fluence in the database summary. The rat study used 660-nm red visible laser light at 4 J/cm², 100 mW, for 1.12 seconds at each of three points, daily for 30 days. These different protocols and delivery geometries have not been compared directly.

Interpretation

The mixed human study reports changes in wound width and length, with the direction depending on the measure and subgroup. It does not show that an anal fistula tract closed or that recurrence was prevented. In rats, PBM reduced tract area and inflammatory findings but did not produce complete closure. The current evidence concerns possible adjunctive effects on postoperative healing, not definitive fistula treatment.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term wound-dimension changes in mixed postoperative anorectal wounds Very low for fistula-tract closure or recurrence prevention
Publications and records2 relevant articles (one narrow perianal-fistula mapping)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

A small controlled postoperative study included fistula wounds among several anorectal conditions and reported greater width reduction in the mixed sample, while length results differed by subgroup and summary. A rat fistula experiment reduced tract area and inflammation but did not close tracts fully. Fistula-specific trials with clear patient counts, closure criteria, and recurrence follow-up are needed.
